title: Reading Aloud Is Not a Soft Option
author: Mary Myatt
summary: Mary Myatt argues, in the context of the UK DfE white paper's expectation that literacy belongs to every teacher in every subject, that reading aloud to pupils is not a pleasant supplement to learning but a form of learning itself. Reporting a conversation with a headteacher whose staff value reading aloud but do not always see it as the best use of their time, Myatt identifies this perception as a structural vulnerability: when reading aloud is framed as 'lovely' rather than substantive, it becomes permanently vulnerable to being displaced by tasks considered more academically serious. Against this, she makes the case that hearing rich texts read aloud gives pupils access to vocabulary, syntax, knowledge, and disciplinary language they could not yet manage independently—making it not a supplement to the curriculum but a route into it. This matters most for pupils who do not arrive at school with large reserves of vocabulary and background knowledge; for these pupils, the curriculum must do more of the heavy lifting, and teachers reading aloud is one of the most direct mechanisms for providing access. Myatt connects this to whole-school literacy strategy: literacy across the curriculum is not about every teacher becoming an English teacher but about every teacher recognizing that pupils cannot think deeply in a subject whose language they cannot access.
points: When reading aloud is perceived as enjoyable but non-essential, it is always vulnerable to being squeezed out by tasks framed as 'proper learning'—a perception that must be replaced by understanding reading aloud as curriculum work, not enrichment.

Reading aloud gives pupils access to vocabulary, syntax, knowledge, and disciplinary language above their independent reading level; for pupils without rich vocabulary reserves, this access is not incidental but structurally necessary for curriculum participation.

Literacy across the curriculum is not about every teacher becoming an English teacher—it is about every teacher recognizing that pupils cannot think deeply in a subject they cannot access linguistically.

The DfE white paper makes cross-curricular literacy a whole-school expectation; for primary leaders, the question is whether their schools have the tools, training, and professional culture to deliver on it—not merely good intentions.

Reading aloud, shared reading, vocabulary teaching, and purposeful writing are part of the route into the curriculum, not extras bolted on—they are the mechanism by which all pupils gain equitable access to deep subject-specific thinking.
quotes: If reading aloud is seen as a lovely thing to do, but not a central part of curriculum work, then it will always be vulnerable. Vulnerable to being squeezed out, to being replaced by another task, or to the idea that 'proper learning' lies elsewhere. But reading to pupils is not a soft option and it's not a pause from learning. It is learning.

When pupils hear rich texts read aloud, they are given access to vocabulary, syntax, knowledge and ideas that they may not yet be able to manage independently. They hear how complex language works. They encounter words in context. They build background knowledge. They experience the rhythm and structure of disciplinary language.

Literacy across the curriculum is not about every teacher becoming an English teacher. It is about every teacher recognising that pupils cannot think deeply in a subject if they cannot access its language.

This is particularly important for pupils who do not arrive at school with large reserves of vocabulary, background knowledge and reading experience. For these pupils, the curriculum has to do more of the heavy lifting.
Reading aloud, shared reading, careful vocabulary teaching and purposeful writing are not extras. They are part of the route into the curriculum.
